subject: physics

items.q: An ice-hockey puck is struck and then slides across horizontal ice. Friction and air resistance on the puck are negligible. What happens to the motion of the puck after it has left the stick?
items.correct: It continues in a straight line at a constant speed.
items.misconception: It slows gradually as the force from the stick is used up.
items.why: The pre-Newtonian 'impetus' idea: a thrown object seems to keep going because it has been given something, which runs out as it slows. Everyday phrases such as 'the force of the ball' and 'absorbing the force' reinforce it. A force is an interaction between two bodies and exists only while they interact. A body carries momentum and kinetic energy, not force. Once contact ends, the thrower exerts no force at all.
items.specStatementText: Newton’s three laws of motion
items.random_wrong: It slows and stops, as moving bodies come to rest naturally.

items.q: A book rests on a horizontal table. The weight of the book is the gravitational force exerted on it by the Earth. Which force forms a Newton's third law pair with this weight?
items.correct: The gravitational force exerted on the Earth by the book
items.misconception: The normal force exerted on the book by the table
items.why: The third law is often quoted as 'every action has an equal and opposite reaction', and the weight and normal force of a resting object are the most familiar equal and opposite forces, so students match them. A third-law pair is the two sides of ONE interaction between TWO bodies: the forces act on different bodies and are of the same type. Forces on the same body can never be a third-law pair, however well they balance.
items.specStatementText: Newton’s three laws of motion
items.random_wrong: The contact force exerted on the table by the book

items.q: A lamp of mass 5.0 kg hangs at rest, supported by two cables, one on each side. Each cable makes an angle of 40° with the horizontal, and the arrangement is symmetrical. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the tension in each cable?
items.why:
It is true for two vertical cables, which is the case students meet first, and 'sharing the load' seems obvious. Students do not resolve the tension into components. Resolve each tension into vertical and horizontal components. The vertical components add to balance the weight; the horizontal components cancel. The shallower the cables, the larger the tension needed.

Working: Translational equilibrium: resultant force = 0. Horizontal components cancel by symmetry. Vertical: 2T sin 40° = mg ⇒ T = mg/(2 sin 40°) = (5.0 kg × 9.8 m s⁻²)/(2 × 0.6428) = 49 N/1.286 = 38 N.
items.specStatementText: Newton’s three laws of motion
items.working: Translational equilibrium: resultant force = 0. Horizontal components cancel by symmetry. Vertical: 2T sin 40° = mg ⇒ T = mg/(2 sin 40°) = (5.0 kg × 9.8 m s⁻²)/(2 × 0.6428) = 49 N/1.286 = 38 N.

items.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. Air resistance is negligible. Which force or forces act on the ball while it is still rising, after it has left the hand?
items.correct: Only its weight, the downward pull of the Earth
items.misconception: Its weight and an upward force larger than its weight
items.why: Everyday experience: a pushed box stops when the pushing stops, because friction acts on it. This is the pre-Newtonian (Aristotelian) view, and it is one of the most widely documented misconceptions in physics education research. Newton's first law: with no resultant force, velocity is constant. Everyday bodies stop because friction or drag is a resultant force opposing their motion; remove those forces and the motion continues unchanged.
items.specStatementText: forces as interactions between bodies
items.random_wrong: Its weight and a decreasing upward force from the throw

items.q: A car of mass 1.2 × 10³ kg travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ collides head-on with a truck of mass 1.2 × 10⁴ kg travelling at 10 m s⁻¹. How does the force exerted by the truck on the car compare with the force exerted by the car on the truck during the collision?
items.correct: They are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
items.misconception: The truck's force is larger, since the truck has more mass.
items.why: Students treat mass as "strength": a bigger, heavier body seems able to push or pull harder, and a very small body seems unable to affect a very large one at all. This "greater mass implies greater force" idea is documented by the Force Concept Inventory. Newton's third law: the two forces of an interaction have equal magnitude whatever the masses. The difference lies in the accelerations: the same force gives a much smaller acceleration to the larger mass.
items.specStatementText: forces as interactions between bodies
items.random_wrong: The car's force is larger, since the car is moving faster.

items.q: A box is pulled at constant velocity across a rough horizontal floor by a rope that makes an angle of 30° above the horizontal. Which list gives all the forces that should appear on a free-body diagram of the box, and no others?
items.correct: Weight, normal force, rope tension and friction from the floor
items.misconception: Weight, normal force, tension, friction, push of box on floor
items.why: Third-law pairs are taught together, so students draw both members of each pair on the same diagram. Diagrams of whole situations, with forces on several bodies, also blur the idea of isolating one body. Choose one body and draw only the forces other bodies exert on it. For each arrow ask 'what exerts this force, and on what?'; if the answer is 'on something else', it does not belong on this diagram.
items.specStatementText: that forces acting on a body can be represented in a free-body diagram
items.random_wrong: Weight, normal force, tension, friction, forward force of motion

items.q: A free-body diagram for a puck on a frictionless horizontal air table shows three horizontal forces: 30 N towards the east, 10 N towards the west and 15 N towards the north. The vertical forces on the puck balance. What is the magnitude of the resultant force on the puck?
items.why:
Adding numbers is the default operation, and the everyday word 'total' suggests simple addition. Students do not yet treat force as a vector. Add forces as vectors: along each direction, forces in opposite senses subtract. Only then combine the perpendicular components, using √(F_x² + F_y²).

Working: Take east and north as positive. F_x = 30 N − 10 N = 20 N; F_y = 15 N. |F| = √(20² + 15²) N = √625 N = 25 N.
items.specStatementText: that free-body diagrams can be analysed to find the resultant force on a system
items.working: Take east and north as positive. F_x = 30 N − 10 N = 20 N; F_y = 15 N. |F| = √(20² + 15²) N = √625 N = 25 N.

items.q: Two blocks, A of mass 5.0 kg and B of mass 7.0 kg, are in contact on a frictionless horizontal surface. A horizontal force of 60 N pushes block A, which in turn pushes block B, and both accelerate together. What is the magnitude of the force that A exerts on B?
items.why:
Students picture force as something passed along a chain, like a message, rather than as separate interactions at each contact. Treat the blocks together to find the common acceleration, a = F/(m_A + m_B), then draw a free-body diagram of B alone: the only horizontal force on B is the push from A, which equals m_B a.

Working: System A + B: a = F/(m_A + m_B) = 60 N/(5.0 + 7.0) kg = 5.0 m s⁻². Block B alone: F_AB = m_B a = 7.0 kg × 5.0 m s⁻² = 35 N. Check with block A: 60 N − 35 N = 25 N = 5.0 kg × 5.0 m s⁻².
items.specStatementText: that free-body diagrams can be analysed to find the resultant force on a system
items.working: System A + B: a = F/(m_A + m_B) = 60 N/(5.0 + 7.0) kg = 5.0 m s⁻². Block B alone: F_AB = m_B a = 7.0 kg × 5.0 m s⁻² = 35 N. Check with block A: 60 N − 35 N = 25 N = 5.0 kg × 5.0 m s⁻².

items.q: A block of mass 4.0 kg slides down a rough plane inclined at 25° to the horizontal. The coefficient of dynamic friction between the block and the plane is 0.20. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the magnitude of the frictional force on the block?
items.why:
For a body resting on a horizontal floor, F_N = mg, and this first example is remembered as a rule. The misconception that weight and normal force are a third-law pair also suggests they must always be equal. Find F_N from the free-body diagram by resolving perpendicular to the surface. Only on a horizontal surface with no other vertical forces and no vertical acceleration does F_N equal mg.

Working: F_N = mg cos θ = 4.0 kg × 9.8 m s⁻² × cos 25° = 39.2 N × 0.9063 = 35.5 N. Sliding, so F_f = μ_d F_N = 0.20 × 35.5 N = 7.1 N.

items.q: A crate of mass 12 kg rests on a horizontal floor. The coefficients of friction between the crate and the floor are μ_s = 0.50 and μ_d = 0.40. A worker pushes horizontally on the crate with a force of 40 N, but the crate does not move. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the frictional force on the crate?
items.correct: 40 N, equal and opposite to the worker's push
items.misconception: 59 N, which is the value of μ_s F_N for the crate
items.why:
The equation F_f = μ F_N is often quoted without the inequality, and students treat every formula as an equality to substitute into. Static friction adjusts to balance the other forces parallel to the surface, up to the limit μ_s F_N. If a 40 N push does not move a crate, friction is 40 N, even if μ_s F_N is larger.

Working: F_N = mg = 12 kg × 9.8 m s⁻² = 117.6 N. Maximum static friction = μ_s F_N = 0.50 × 117.6 N = 58.8 N. Push 40 N < 58.8 N, so the crate stays at rest; equilibrium gives F_f = 40 N, opposite to the push.

items.q: A spring of spring constant k = 40 N m⁻¹ has a natural length of 10.0 cm. One end is fixed and a student pulls the other end so that the length of the spring becomes 13.0 cm. Taking the direction in which the spring is stretched as positive, what is the elastic restoring force F_H that the spring exerts on the student's hand?
items.why:
Students usually calculate only the magnitude kx, and 'the spring is pulled to the right' is misread as 'the spring force is to the right'. A stretched spring pulls back towards its natural length; a compressed spring pushes out towards it. With the extension taken as positive, F_H is negative.

Working: x = 13.0 cm − 10.0 cm = 3.0 cm = 0.030 m (positive, in the direction of stretching). F_H = −kx = −(40 N m⁻¹)(0.030 m) = −1.2 N, i.e. 1.2 N directed opposite to the extension.

items.q: A small steel sphere of diameter 2.0 mm is released in a tall tube of glycerol and falls at terminal velocity. The weight of the sphere is 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ N and its volume is 4.2 × 10⁻⁹ m³. The density of glycerol is 1.3 × 10³ kg m⁻³ and its viscosity is 1.4 Pa s. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the terminal velocity of the sphere?
items.why:
In everyday language 'buoyant' means 'able to float', so students link buoyancy only to floating. Buoyancy depends on the fluid displaced, not on whether the body floats. For a sphere falling through a liquid, buoyancy acts upwards alongside the drag, and both must be included in the terminal-velocity condition.

Working: Terminal velocity: F_g = F_b + F_d. F_b = ρVg = (1.3 × 10³ kg m⁻³)(4.2 × 10⁻⁹ m³)(9.8 m s⁻²) = 5.35 × 10⁻⁵ N. F_d = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ N − 5.35 × 10⁻⁵ N = 2.67 × 10⁻⁴ N. r = 1.0 mm = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m. v = F_d/(6πηr) = 2.67 × 10⁻⁴ N/(6π × 1.4 Pa s × 1.0 × 10⁻³ m) = 2.67 × 10⁻⁴/2.64 × 10⁻² = 1.0 × 10⁻² m s⁻¹.

items.q: A solid steel sphere and a solid aluminium sphere have the same volume. Both hang from threads, completely under water: the steel sphere 0.20 m below the surface and the aluminium sphere 0.50 m below it. Steel is about three times as dense as aluminium. How do the buoyancy forces on the two spheres compare?
items.correct: They are equal, as each sphere displaces the same volume of water
items.misconception: It is larger on the steel sphere, as steel is the denser metal
items.why: Students confuse the buoyancy force with whether the body floats, which does depend on the body's density, and often substitute the body's density for ρ in F_b = ρVg. Buoyancy is the weight of fluid displaced. What differs between a steel and an aluminium sphere of equal volume is their weight, so the resultant force differs, not the buoyancy.

items.q: An astronaut has a mass of 70.0 kg on Earth, where g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹. She travels to the Moon, where g = 1.62 N kg⁻¹. Which statement about the astronaut on the Moon is correct?
items.correct: Her weight is 113 N.
items.misconception: Her weight is 686 N.
items.why:
In everyday language 'weight' means mass, measured in kilograms ('my weight is 70 kg'), so students treat weight as an unchanging property. Mass (kg) is a property of the body. Weight (N) is the force of gravity on it, F_g = mg, and changes when g changes.

Working: Mass is independent of location: m = 70.0 kg on the Moon. Weight on the Moon: F_g = mg = 70.0 kg × 1.62 N kg⁻¹ = 113.4 N ≈ 113 N (on Earth it is 70.0 × 9.8 = 686 N).
items.specStatementText: the nature and use of the following field forces ◦ gravitational force F_g is the weight of the body and calculated is given by F_g = mg ◦ electric force F_e ◦ magnetic force F_m
items.random_wrong: Her mass is reduced.
items.working: Mass is independent of location: m = 70.0 kg on the Moon. Weight on the Moon: F_g = mg = 70.0 kg × 1.62 N kg⁻¹ = 113.4 N ≈ 113 N (on Earth it is 70.0 × 9.8 = 686 N).

items.q: Which statement about field forces is correct?
items.correct: An electric field exerts a force on a charged particle even when it is at rest.
items.misconception: A magnetic field exerts a force on a charged particle even when it is at rest.
items.why: Students generalise from magnets attracting iron and from electric forces on charges, and treat magnetic and electric fields as acting on charges in the same way. Electric force: acts on any charge in an electric field. Magnetic force: acts only on charges moving through a magnetic field (and not moving parallel to it). A stationary charge in a magnetic field experiences no magnetic force.
items.specStatementText: the nature and use of the following field forces ◦ gravitational force F_g is the weight of the body and calculated is given by F_g = mg ◦ electric force F_e ◦ magnetic force F_m
items.random_wrong: A gravitational force acts on a body only where there is air around it.

items.q: A ball is released from rest and falls towards the ground. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement about momentum during the fall is correct?
items.correct: The ball's momentum increases, while the total momentum of the ball and the Earth stays constant.
items.misconception: The ball's momentum stays constant, because momentum is conserved in every situation.
items.why: The law is often stated briefly as 'momentum is conserved' without the condition or the word 'total', so students apply it to single bodies. State the system and the condition: the total momentum of a system is constant when no resultant external force acts on the system. A falling ball's momentum increases; the ball–Earth system's does not change.
items.specStatementText: that linear momentum as given by p = mv remains constant unless the system is acted upon by a resultant external force
items.random_wrong: The ball's momentum stays constant, because its gain in E_k equals its loss in E_p.

items.q: Under which condition does the total momentum of a system of interacting bodies remain constant?
items.correct: When no resultant external force acts on the system
items.misconception: When every collision between the bodies is elastic
items.why: Both laws are 'conservation laws' taught close together and both are used in collision problems, so students merge them. Test the two separately. Momentum: is there a resultant external force? Kinetic energy: compare ½mv² totals before and after. In an inelastic collision momentum is conserved while kinetic energy is not.
items.specStatementText: that linear momentum as given by p = mv remains constant unless the system is acted upon by a resultant external force
items.random_wrong: When the bodies exert no forces at all on one another

items.q: A crate on a rough horizontal floor is pushed horizontally with a constant force of 40.0 N for 5.00 s. Throughout this time the crate slides forwards and the dynamic frictional force on it is 15.0 N. What is the magnitude of the impulse delivered to the crate by the resultant force during the 5.00 s?
items.correct: 125 N s
items.misconception: 200 N s
items.why:
Questions usually highlight one applied force, and students use it without asking what the resultant force is. Draw the free-body diagram, find the resultant force and use J = FΔt with that resultant. Only the resultant impulse equals the change in momentum.

Working: Resultant force F = 40.0 N − 15.0 N = 25.0 N (forwards). J = FΔt = 25.0 N × 5.00 s = 125 N s.
items.specStatementText: that a resultant external force applied to a system constitutes an impulse J as given by J = FΔt where F is the average resultant force and Δt is the time of contact
items.random_wrong: 275 N s
items.working: Resultant force F = 40.0 N − 15.0 N = 25.0 N (forwards). J = FΔt = 25.0 N × 5.00 s = 125 N s.

items.q: A ball of mass 0.060 kg moving at 30 m s⁻¹ strikes a wall at right angles and rebounds along the same line at 20 m s⁻¹. Taking the direction towards the wall as positive, what impulse does the wall exert on the ball?
items.why:
Students associate momentum with the direction of motion and assume its change points the same way. Calculate Δp = m(v − u) with signs. For a ball moving towards a wall (+) and bouncing back (−), Δp is negative: the wall pushes the ball away from it.

Working: J = Δp = m(v − u) with u = +30 m s⁻¹ and v = −20 m s⁻¹: J = 0.060 kg × (−20 − 30) m s⁻¹ = 0.060 × (−50) = −3.0 N s (3.0 N s away from the wall).
items.specStatementText: that the applied external impulse equals the change in momentum of the system
items.working: J = Δp = m(v − u) with u = +30 m s⁻¹ and v = −20 m s⁻¹: J = 0.060 kg × (−20 − 30) m s⁻¹ = 0.060 × (−50) = −3.0 N s (3.0 N s away from the wall).

items.q: Two identical eggs are dropped from the same height. One lands on a thick foam cushion and stops without breaking; the other lands on a concrete floor, stops and breaks. Neither egg bounces. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Each egg receives the same impulse, but the foam acts for longer, so the average force is smaller.
items.misconception: The foam reduces the egg's change in momentum, so the average force exerted on it is smaller.
items.why: Students know that cushions reduce damage and link this to reducing the quantities in the equation they have just learned, not to the time over which the change happens. With Δp fixed by the initial and final velocities, F = Δp/Δt: a longer Δt gives a smaller average force. This is how airbags, crumple zones and landing mats work.
items.specStatementText: that the applied external impulse equals the change in momentum of the system
items.random_wrong: The foam absorbs the force of the falling egg, so less force is left to act on the egg's shell.

items.q: Sand falls vertically onto a horizontal conveyor belt at a steady rate of 0.80 kg s⁻¹. The belt moves at a constant 2.5 m s⁻¹, and the sand quickly reaches the speed of the belt. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the horizontal force that the belt exerts on the sand?
items.why:
F = ma is the form of the second law students use most, and it gives F = 0 whenever a = 0; the assumption of constant mass is hidden. Use F = Δp/Δt. When mass changes, momentum changes even at constant velocity, because Δp = vΔm. F = ma is valid only when mass is constant.

Working: F = Δp/Δt. Horizontal momentum gained per second = (Δm/Δt) × v = 0.80 kg s⁻¹ × 2.5 m s⁻¹ = 2.0 kg m s⁻² = 2.0 N. (F = ma would give zero because the belt's velocity is constant, but the mass being moved is not constant.)
items.specStatementText: that Newton’s second law in the form F = ma assumes mass is constant whereas F = Δp/Δt allows for situations where mass is changing
items.working: F = Δp/Δt. Horizontal momentum gained per second = (Δm/Δt) × v = 0.80 kg s⁻¹ × 2.5 m s⁻¹ = 2.0 kg m s⁻² = 2.0 N. (F = ma would give zero because the belt's velocity is constant, but the mass being moved is not constant.)

items.q: Which statement describes an elastic collision between two bodies?
items.correct: The total kinetic energy of the two bodies is the same before and after.
items.misconception: The bodies bounce apart after colliding, instead of sticking together.
items.why: The two textbook extremes are 'bouncing' and 'sticking', and the everyday meaning of elastic ('springy') links it to bouncing. Classify collisions by kinetic energy: elastic if total E_k is conserved, inelastic if it decreases. Sticking together is the special case of a totally inelastic collision.
items.specStatementText: the elastic and inelastic collisions of two bodies
items.random_wrong: At least one of the bodies is made of a stretchy material such as rubber.

items.q: A trolley of mass 1.2 kg moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ along a straight horizontal track collides with a stationary trolley of mass 0.80 kg. The trolleys stick together. Friction is negligible. What is their speed immediately after the collision?
items.correct: 1.8 m s⁻¹
items.misconception: 1.5 m s⁻¹
items.why:
'Sharing' suggests averaging, and the rule happens to work when the two masses are equal, which is the first example students often see. Apply momentum conservation with both masses: total momentum before = (total mass) × (common velocity).

Working: p before = 1.2 kg × 3.0 m s⁻¹ + 0 = 3.6 kg m s⁻¹. p after = (1.2 + 0.80) kg × v. v = 3.6/2.0 = 1.8 m s⁻¹, in the original direction.
items.specStatementText: the elastic and inelastic collisions of two bodies
items.random_wrong: 4.5 m s⁻¹
items.working: p before = 1.2 kg × 3.0 m s⁻¹ + 0 = 3.6 kg m s⁻¹. p after = (1.2 + 0.80) kg × v. v = 3.6/2.0 = 1.8 m s⁻¹, in the original direction.

items.q: A ball of mass 0.50 kg moving at 4.0 m s⁻¹ collides head-on with a stationary ball of mass 1.5 kg. After the collision, the 0.50 kg ball moves back along its original line at 2.0 m s⁻¹ and the 1.5 kg ball moves forwards at 2.0 m s⁻¹. Which conclusion about the collision is correct?
items.correct: It is elastic: the total kinetic energy is 4.0 J before and after.
items.misconception: It is impossible: the momentum after is 4.0 kg m s⁻¹, not 2.0.
items.why:
Students calculate p = mv with speeds, as they would E_k, and do not assign signs for direction. Choose a positive direction and give every velocity, and therefore every momentum, a sign. Two bodies moving apart in opposite directions can have zero total momentum.

Working: Take the initial direction as positive. p before = 0.50 × 4.0 = 2.0 kg m s⁻¹; p after = 0.50 × (−2.0) + 1.5 × (+2.0) = −1.0 + 3.0 = 2.0 kg m s⁻¹ (conserved). E_k before = ½ × 0.50 × 4.0² = 4.0 J; E_k after = ½ × 0.50 × 2.0² + ½ × 1.5 × 2.0² = 1.0 J + 3.0 J = 4.0 J. Total E_k unchanged ⇒ elastic.
items.specStatementText: the elastic and inelastic collisions of two bodies
items.random_wrong: It is inelastic, because the kinetic energy of the 0.50 kg ball decreased.
items.working: Take the initial direction as positive. p before = 0.50 × 4.0 = 2.0 kg m s⁻¹; p after = 0.50 × (−2.0) + 1.5 × (+2.0) = −1.0 + 3.0 = 2.0 kg m s⁻¹ (conserved). E_k before = ½ × 0.50 × 4.0² = 4.0 J; E_k after = ½ × 0.50 × 2.0² + ½ × 1.5 × 2.0² = 1.0 J + 3.0 J = 4.0 J. Total E_k unchanged ⇒ elastic.

items.q: Two ice skaters stand at rest facing each other on smooth ice. Skater A, of mass 60 kg, pushes skater B, of mass 45 kg, and they move apart in opposite directions along a straight line. Immediately afterwards B moves at 2.0 m s⁻¹. Friction is negligible. What is the speed of A?
items.correct: 1.5 m s⁻¹
items.misconception: 2.0 m s⁻¹
items.why:
Students correctly apply Newton's third law to the forces and then assume the effects (speeds) are also equal, without dividing by the masses. Equal impulses give equal magnitudes of momentum change. Divide by each mass to find the speeds: the lighter body moves faster.

Working: Total momentum before = 0. After: m_A v_A + m_B v_B = 0 ⇒ 60 kg × v_A = −45 kg × 2.0 m s⁻¹ ⇒ v_A = −1.5 m s⁻¹, a speed of 1.5 m s⁻¹ opposite to B.
items.specStatementText: explosions
items.random_wrong: 1.7 m s⁻¹
items.working: Total momentum before = 0. After: m_A v_A + m_B v_B = 0 ⇒ 60 kg × v_A = −45 kg × 2.0 m s⁻¹ ⇒ v_A = −1.5 m s⁻¹, a speed of 1.5 m s⁻¹ opposite to B.

items.q: A trolley of mass 0.50 kg moving at 6.0 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary trolley of mass 1.0 kg on a straight, frictionless track. The trolleys stick together and move off at 2.0 m s⁻¹. How much kinetic energy is transferred to other forms in the collision?
items.why:
Students know that energy is always conserved and do not distinguish total energy from the kinetic store. In a collision, total momentum and total energy are conserved; kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions. Momentum, not kinetic energy, is used to find velocities in inelastic collisions.

Working: Momentum check: 0.50 × 6.0 = 3.0 kg m s⁻¹ = 1.5 × 2.0. E_k before = ½ × 0.50 kg × (6.0 m s⁻¹)² = 9.0 J. E_k after = ½ × 1.5 kg × (2.0 m s⁻¹)² = 3.0 J. Transferred = 9.0 J − 3.0 J = 6.0 J.
items.specStatementText: energy considerations in elastic collisions, inelastic collisions, and explosions
items.working: Momentum check: 0.50 × 6.0 = 3.0 kg m s⁻¹ = 1.5 × 2.0. E_k before = ½ × 0.50 kg × (6.0 m s⁻¹)² = 9.0 J. E_k after = ½ × 1.5 kg × (2.0 m s⁻¹)² = 3.0 J. Transferred = 9.0 J − 3.0 J = 6.0 J.

items.q: A firework shell is at rest when it explodes into several fragments. External forces can be ignored during the explosion. Which statement about the fragments immediately after the explosion is correct?
items.correct: Their total momentum is zero and their total kinetic energy has increased.
items.misconception: Their total momentum has increased, as has their total kinetic energy.
items.why: Students see motion appear from rest and associate motion with momentum, forgetting that momentum is a vector whose total can stay zero. Add the fragments' momenta as vectors. Equal and opposite internal forces give equal and opposite impulses, so the total momentum does not change.
items.specStatementText: energy considerations in elastic collisions, inelastic collisions, and explosions
items.random_wrong: Their total momentum is zero, and so is their total kinetic energy.

items.q: The drum of a washing machine has a diameter of 0.50 m. It rotates about a horizontal axis at constant speed, with a time period of 0.050 s. What is the centripetal acceleration of a sock pressed against the inside of the drum?
items.why:
v = 2πr/T, the first circular-motion relation students meet, is inversely proportional to T. Students carry that proportionality over to a without seeing that a = v²/r squares it, and a unit check is rarely done. Derive the formula from a = v²/r with v = 2πr/T, and check units: m ÷ s² gives m s⁻², but m ÷ s does not.

Working: r = 0.50 m/2 = 0.25 m. a = 4π²r/T² = 4π² × 0.25 m/(0.050 s)² = 9.87 m/2.5 × 10⁻³ s² = 3.9 × 10³ m s⁻². (Equivalently v = 2πr/T = 31.4 m s⁻¹ and a = v²/r = 3.9 × 10³ m s⁻².)
items.specStatementText: that bodies moving along a circular trajectory at a constant speed experience an acceleration that is directed radially towards the centre of the circle—known as a centripetal acceleration as given by a = v²/r = ω²r = 4π²r/T²
items.working: r = 0.50 m/2 = 0.25 m. a = 4π²r/T² = 4π² × 0.25 m/(0.050 s)² = 9.87 m/2.5 × 10⁻³ s² = 3.9 × 10³ m s⁻². (Equivalently v = 2πr/T = 31.4 m s⁻¹ and a = v²/r = 3.9 × 10³ m s⁻².)

items.q: A car travels at constant speed around a bend on a flat horizontal road; its path is part of a horizontal circle. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement about the horizontal forces on the car is correct?
items.correct: Friction from the road acts towards the centre and is the resultant force.
items.misconception: Friction acts towards the centre and is balanced by a centrifugal force.
items.why: Passengers feel thrown outwards on a bend, and the word 'centrifugal' is used in everyday language and for machines such as spin driers. Objects on a turntable or in a spinning drum seem to be flung outwards, which looks like the effect of an outward resultant force. A body moving in a circle is not in equilibrium: the resultant force is inwards, and it causes the centripetal acceleration. Without that inward force the body would move off along a tangent, not outwards along a radius.
items.specStatementText: that circular motion is caused by a centripetal force acting perpendicular to the velocity
items.random_wrong: Friction and a separate centripetal force both act towards the centre.

items.q: A small ball of mass 0.30 kg on a string of length 0.60 m swings as a pendulum in a vertical plane. As it passes through its lowest point its speed is 2.8 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the tension in the string at this point?
items.why:
In horizontal circular motion on a frictionless table the tension alone does provide the centripetal force, and students carry this over to vertical circles. Draw the free-body diagram at the point in question. At the lowest point, tension acts up (towards the centre) and weight acts down (away from it): T − mg = mv²/r.

Working: At the lowest point, taking towards the centre (upwards) as positive: T − mg = mv²/r. T = mg + mv²/r = 0.30 × 9.8 N + 0.30 × (2.8)²/0.60 N = 2.94 N + 3.92 N = 6.86 N ≈ 6.9 N.
items.specStatementText: that circular motion is caused by a centripetal force acting perpendicular to the velocity
items.working: At the lowest point, taking towards the centre (upwards) as positive: T − mg = mv²/r. T = mg + mv²/r = 0.30 × 9.8 N + 0.30 × (2.8)²/0.60 N = 2.94 N + 3.92 N = 6.86 N ≈ 6.9 N.

items.q: A cyclist rides around a flat circular track at a constant speed of 8.0 m s⁻¹. Which statement about her motion is correct?
items.correct: Her velocity changes, so a resultant force acts towards the centre.
items.misconception: Her velocity is constant, so the resultant force acting on her is zero.
items.why: In everyday language speed and velocity mean the same thing, and 'acceleration' means 'speeding up'. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, including a change of direction. A body moving along a circle at constant speed has centripetal acceleration v²/r.
items.specStatementText: that a centripetal force causes the body to change direction even if its magnitude of velocity may remain constant
items.random_wrong: A resultant force acts on her outwards, away from the centre of the track.

items.q: A bicycle wheel of diameter 0.700 m rotates at a steady rate about a fixed axle, making one complete revolution every 0.250 s. What is the linear speed of a point on the rim of the wheel?
items.why:
Many questions state the diameter because it is what is measured, and students substitute the number given without checking which quantity the equation needs. Halve the diameter to get r before substituting. Using the diameter gives an answer too large or too small by a factor of 2 (or 4 where r is squared).

Working: r = 0.700 m/2 = 0.350 m. ω = 2π/T = 2π/0.250 s = 25.1 rad s⁻¹. v = ωr = 25.1 rad s⁻¹ × 0.350 m = 8.80 m s⁻¹ (= 2πr/T).
items.specStatementText: that the motion along a circular trajectory can be described in terms of the angular velocity ω which is related to the linear speed v by the equation as given by v = 2πr/T = ωr.

items.q: A person stands on the floor of a lift that is accelerating upwards. Which description of a correct free-body diagram for the person is right?
items.correct: Two arrows: the weight downwards and a larger normal force from the floor upwards.
items.misconception: Two arrows: the weight downwards and a normal force of equal size from the floor upwards.
items.why: For a body resting on a horizontal floor, F_N = mg, and this first example is remembered as a rule. The misconception that weight and normal force are a third-law pair also suggests they must always be equal. Find F_N from the free-body diagram by resolving perpendicular to the surface. Only on a horizontal surface with no other vertical forces and no vertical acceleration does F_N equal mg.
items.specStatementText: that forces acting on a body can be represented in a free-body diagram
items.random_wrong: Three arrows: the weight, the normal force, and an upward force of the lift's motion.

items.q: A cricket ball is struck by a bat. During the short time of contact the force between the bat and the ball rises from zero to a maximum and then falls back to zero. Which statement about the impulse delivered to the ball is correct?
items.correct: It is the product of the average resultant force on the ball and the time of contact.
items.misconception: It is the product of the maximum force exerted on the ball and the total time of contact.
items.why: Worked examples usually quote a single value for 'the force', so a student multiplies the one number given (often the peak) by the time; the rectangle F_max × Δt is also the easiest area to read from a graph. Impulse is the area under the force–time graph. For a triangular pulse it is ½ F_max Δt; in general it is F_average × Δt, where the average is taken over the whole contact.
items.specStatementText: that a resultant external force applied to a system constitutes an impulse J as given by J = FΔt where F is the average resultant force and Δt is the time of contact
items.random_wrong: It is the largest value reached by the resultant force on the ball during the contact.

items.q: A rocket travels through deep space, far from any star or planet. Its engine ejects exhaust gas backwards at a constant rate and at a constant speed relative to the rocket. Which statement about the acceleration of the rocket while the engine is firing is correct?
items.correct: It increases, because the mass of the rocket keeps decreasing as fuel is used up.
items.misconception: It is zero, because there is nothing in empty space for the exhaust gas to push against.
items.why: Everyday propulsion (walking, swimming, a propeller) does push on an external medium, so the idea is generalised to all propulsion; the force pair between the rocket and its own exhaust is not recognised as an interaction between two bodies. The interaction is between the rocket and the gas it ejects. The force on the gas (backwards) and the force on the rocket (forwards) are a Newton's third law pair. Air, if present, only adds drag.
items.specStatementText: that Newton’s second law in the form F = ma assumes mass is constant whereas F = Δp/Δt allows for situations where mass is changing
items.random_wrong: It stays constant, because a constant thrust produces a constant acceleration.

items.q: A body at rest on a smooth horizontal surface explodes into two pieces, of masses m and 3m, which move apart along a straight line. External forces are negligible during the explosion. Which statement about the pieces immediately after the explosion is correct?
items.correct: The lighter piece moves away three times as fast as the heavier piece does.
items.misconception: The two pieces carry equal kinetic energies, as the energy is shared out equally.
items.why: The symmetry of 'equal and opposite' momenta is extended to energy, and sharing equally feels fair and natural. Use momentum conservation to find the velocities first; then calculate each part's E_k. With equal momenta, E_k = p²/2m is largest for the smallest mass.
items.specStatementText: explosions
items.random_wrong: The two pieces move apart with equal speeds, as the forces on them were equal.

items.q: A body moves in uniform circular motion. Which single change would double its centripetal acceleration?
items.correct: Halving the radius while keeping the speed the same
items.misconception: Doubling the speed while keeping the radius the same
items.why: The square is dropped when the formula is recalled by analogy with ω = v/r, and the everyday intuition that 'twice as fast means twice the effect' is linear. a = v²/r: at fixed radius, doubling v multiplies the acceleration (and the centripetal force needed) by four. A unit check helps: (m s⁻¹)² / m = m s⁻², whereas v/r has unit s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: that bodies moving along a circular trajectory at a constant speed experience an acceleration that is directed radially towards the centre of the circle—known as a centripetal acceleration as given by a = v²/r = ω²r = 4π²r/T²
items.random_wrong: Doubling the radius, with the speed unchanged

items.q: A car moves around a horizontal circular track and its speed is increasing. Which statement about the resultant force on the car is correct?
items.correct: It has a component towards the centre and a component along the direction of motion.
items.misconception: It points directly towards the centre, whatever the speed of the car is doing.
items.why: Circular motion is introduced through uniform circular motion, where the resultant is exactly centripetal, and the label 'centripetal force' is then taken as a rule for every circular path. Split the acceleration into two parts: a centripetal part, v²/r, which changes the direction of motion, and a tangential part, which changes the speed. Only the first is present in uniform circular motion.
items.specStatementText: that a centripetal force causes the body to change direction even if its magnitude of velocity may remain constant
items.random_wrong: It points directly along the direction of motion, because the car is speeding up.

items.q: A disc rotates at a steady rate about its centre, completing 3.0 revolutions in 2.0 s. A mark on the disc is 0.15 m from the centre. What is the angular velocity of the disc?
items.correct: 9.4 rad s⁻¹
items.misconception: 1.5 rad s⁻¹
items.why:
Rotation rates are quoted in everyday life in revolutions per minute or per second, and the radian is unfamiliar, so the frequency is taken to be the angular velocity. ω is the angle turned through per second, in radians. Convert revolutions to radians with the factor 2π: ω = 2πf. In v = ωr the radian measure is essential.

Working: Frequency f = 3.0 rev / 2.0 s = 1.5 rev s⁻¹, so T = 1/f = 0.67 s. ω = 2π/T = 2πf = 2π × 1.5 = 9.42 rad s⁻¹ ≈ 9.4 rad s⁻¹. (The radius is not needed for ω; the linear speed of the mark would be v = ωr = 9.42 × 0.15 = 1.4 m s⁻¹.)
items.specStatementText: that the motion along a circular trajectory can be described in terms of the angular velocity ω which is related to the linear speed v by the equation as given by v = 2πr/T = ωr.
items.random_wrong: 540 rad s⁻¹
items.working: Frequency f = 3.0 rev / 2.0 s = 1.5 rev s⁻¹, so T = 1/f = 0.67 s. ω = 2π/T = 2πf = 2π × 1.5 = 9.42 rad s⁻¹ ≈ 9.4 rad s⁻¹. (The radius is not needed for ω; the linear speed of the mark would be v = ωr = 9.42 × 0.15 = 1.4 m s⁻¹.)

items.q: The diagram shows a free-body diagram drawn by a student for a block at rest on a rough slope. Which statement about the diagram is correct?
items.correct: F_N is wrongly drawn: it should be perpendicular to the surface of the slope.
items.misconception: The diagram is correct as drawn: F_N acts vertically so that it balances W.
items.why: Almost every early example uses a horizontal surface, where the normal force really is vertical and equal to the weight, so the arrow is memorised as 'the upward force'; the word 'normal' is not connected with 'perpendicular to the surface'. 'Normal' means perpendicular to the surface. On a slope of angle θ the normal force is tilted by θ from the vertical, and for a block at rest it has magnitude mg cos θ; the weight is balanced by F_N and the friction along the slope together.
items.specStatementText: that forces acting on a body can be represented in a free-body diagram
items.random_wrong: F_f should be removed from the diagram, because the block is not sliding.

items.q: The diagram shows the forces acting on a sledge that is being pulled along level snow by a rope. What is the magnitude of the resultant force on the sledge?
items.why:
Resolution is often first taught as "component = F cos θ", so some students use cos for every component, whatever line the angle is measured from. Others memorise "horizontal = cos, vertical = sin" from projectile problems and apply it when the angle is measured from a different line, such as a slope. In both cases a rote rule replaces finding the side adjacent to the angle. Always find the component adjacent to the given angle: it is F cos θ. Check with a limiting case: as θ → 0 the adjacent component should approach F.

Working: Vertical: F_N + T sin 30.0° − W = 55.0 + 25.0 − 80.0 = 0, so the vertical forces balance. Horizontal: T cos 30.0° − F_f = 50.0 × 0.866 − 20.0 = 43.3 − 20.0 = 23.3 N. The resultant is 23.3 N, horizontal, in the direction of travel.
items.specStatementText: that free-body diagrams can be analysed to find the resultant force on a system
items.working: Vertical: F_N + T sin 30.0° − W = 55.0 + 25.0 − 80.0 = 0, so the vertical forces balance. Horizontal: T cos 30.0° − F_f = 50.0 × 0.866 − 20.0 = 43.3 − 20.0 = 23.3 N. The resultant is 23.3 N, horizontal, in the direction of travel.

items.q: The graph shows how the resultant force on a trolley varies with time while it is being pushed. What is the impulse delivered to the trolley during the 0.80 s?
items.correct: 16 N s
items.misconception: 40 N s
items.why:
In everyday English an 'impulse' is a sudden push or kick, and some textbooks speak of an 'impulsive force', so the impulse and the force that produces it are merged into one idea. Keep the two quantities apart by their units: force in N, impulse in N s. The impulse is the accumulated effect of the force over the contact time and equals the change in momentum.

Working: Impulse = area under the F–t graph = area of the triangle = ½ × base × height = ½ × 0.80 s × 40 N = 16 N s. Equivalently the average force is ½ × 40 = 20 N and J = 20 N × 0.80 s = 16 N s.
items.specStatementText: that a resultant external force applied to a system constitutes an impulse J as given by J = FΔt where F is the average resultant force and Δt is the time of contact
items.random_wrong: 32 N s

items.q: Trolley A collides with trolley B, which was at rest, on a frictionless straight track. The graph shows the momentum of each trolley against time. Which conclusion is supported by the graph?
items.correct: The impulses on A and B are equal and opposite, because the force pair acts for the same time.
items.misconception: A exerts a larger force on B than B exerts on A, because A was the moving trolley.
items.why: Students picture the moving or pushing body as the 'cause' and the other as passive, and so assign the force to the cause. The idea that 'the most active agent produces the greatest force' is documented in Force Concept Inventory studies. Newton's third law applies to every interaction: if A pushes B, B pushes A with an equal force. A skater who pushes another skater moves backwards; a fast car and a slow truck exert equal forces on each other.
items.specStatementText: that the applied external impulse equals the change in momentum of the system
items.random_wrong: The collision must be elastic, because the total momentum is the same before and after.

items.q: Trolley A, of mass 1.0 kg, moves along a straight frictionless track and collides head-on with trolley B, which is at rest. The graph shows the velocity of each trolley against time, with A's initial direction taken as positive. What is the mass of trolley B?
items.correct: 2.0 kg
items.misconception: 1.6 kg
items.why:
Students focus on the stationary body 'being set in motion' and forget that the first body is still moving with it. Write momentum after = (m₁ + m₂)v for a combined body. Check that v lies between the two initial velocities.

Working: From the graph: u_A = 4.0 m s⁻¹, v_A = −1.0 m s⁻¹ (A rebounds), u_B = 0, v_B = 2.5 m s⁻¹. Conservation of momentum: m_A u_A = m_A v_A + m_B v_B → 1.0 × 4.0 = 1.0 × (−1.0) + m_B × 2.5 → m_B = 5.0 / 2.5 = 2.0 kg.
items.specStatementText: the elastic and inelastic collisions of two bodies
items.random_wrong: 1.2 kg

items.q: The diagram shows the forces acting on a block at rest on a rough slope. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the slope is 0.70. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the magnitude of the frictional force F_f on the block?
items.why:
Resolution is often first taught as "component = F cos θ", so some students use cos for every component, whatever line the angle is measured from. Others memorise "horizontal = cos, vertical = sin" from projectile problems and apply it when the angle is measured from a different line, such as a slope. In both cases a rote rule replaces finding the side adjacent to the angle. Always find the component adjacent to the given angle: it is F cos θ. Check with a limiting case: as θ → 0 the adjacent component should approach F.

Working: The block is in equilibrium, so along the slope F_f = mg sin 30° = 3.0 × 9.8 × 0.50 = 14.7 N ≈ 15 N (up the slope). Check it is possible: F_N = mg cos 30° = 25.5 N, so the maximum static friction is μ_s F_N = 0.70 × 25.5 = 17.8 N, which exceeds 14.7 N — the block can indeed stay at rest.
items.specStatementText: the nature and use of the following contact forces ◦ normal force F_N is the component of the contact force acting perpendicular to the surface that counteracts the body ◦ surface frictional force F_f acting in a direction parallel to the plane of contact between a body and a surface, on a stationary body as given by F_f ≤ μ_s F_N or a body in motion as given by F_f = μ_d F_N where μ_s and μ_d are the coefficients of static and dynamic friction respectively ◦ tension ◦ elastic restoring force F_H following Hooke’s law as given by F_H = −kx where k is the spring constant ◦ viscous drag force F_d acting on a small sphere opposing its motion through a fluid as given by F_d = 6πηrv where η is the fluid viscosity, r is the radius of the sphere and v is the velocity of the sphere through the fluid ◦ buoyancy F_b acting on a body due to the displacement of the fluid as given by F_b = ρVg where V is the volume of fluid displaced
items.working: The block is in equilibrium, so along the slope F_f = mg sin 30° = 3.0 × 9.8 × 0.50 = 14.7 N ≈ 15 N (up the slope). Check it is possible: F_N = mg cos 30° = 25.5 N, so the maximum static friction is μ_s F_N = 0.70 × 25.5 = 17.8 N, which exceeds 14.7 N — the block can indeed stay at rest.

items.q: A student draws the diagram shown for a ball on a string as it passes through the lowest point of a vertical circle. Which statement about the student's diagram is correct?
items.correct: F_c should be removed; only T and W act on the ball.
items.misconception: F_c is right but should point upwards, towards the centre.
items.why: It is taught with its own name and formula, F = mv²/r, like weight or friction, so students treat it as another force of the same kind. Draw only the real forces. Then find their resultant towards the centre and set it equal to mv²/r.

items.q: A ball on a string moves anticlockwise in a horizontal circle on a smooth table. The string suddenly breaks when the ball is at the point shown in the diagram. Which path does the ball follow after the string breaks?
items.correct: Path A
items.misconception: Path B
items.why: This 'curvilinear impetus' belief is well documented in physics-education research: motion is thought of as a property carried by the body that fades gradually, so curved motion is expected to persist and straighten out slowly. Curving requires a force towards the centre at every instant. Remove the force and the direction stops changing: the ball leaves along the tangent, not along a curve and not radially outwards.
items.specStatementText: that a centripetal force causes the body to change direction even if its magnitude of velocity may remain constant
items.random_wrong: Path C

items.q: Is rest the natural state that every moving body returns to?
items.correct: No. Rest and uniform motion are equally 'natural': both are what happens when the resultant force is zero.
items.misconception: Every moving body naturally slows down and comes to rest, even when no force acts on it.
items.why: Almost every moving object students see eventually stops, and the forces that stop it (friction, air resistance) are invisible, so slowing down seems to need no cause. A body slows down only if a resultant force acts against its motion. A spacecraft coasting far from other bodies, or a puck on almost frictionless ice, keeps moving with nearly constant velocity.

items.q: Is the tension in a string supporting a body always equal to the body's weight?
items.correct: No. Tension equals weight only for a single vertical string holding a body in equilibrium. It is different when strings are at an angle, when several strings share the load or when the body accelerates (including in circular motion).
items.misconception: The tension in a string holding a body is always equal to the body's weight.
items.why: The first tension problem students meet is a mass hanging at rest from a vertical string, where T = mg, and the result is then remembered as a rule. Find tension from the free-body diagram of the body: apply the equilibrium condition, or Newton's second law if the body accelerates, including the centripetal acceleration of a body moving along a circle.

items.q: Is the downward push of a book on a table the same force as the book's weight?
items.correct: No. The weight is the gravitational force of the Earth ON the book. The push of the book on the table is a contact force exerted BY the book; it is the third-law partner of the table's normal force on the book.
items.misconception: A body's weight acts on whatever supports it, so the book's downward push on the table is treated as the weight itself, or as the weight's third-law partner.
items.why: Everyday language says a body 'puts its weight on' a surface, and scales that 'measure weight' actually measure the push on them, so the two forces are treated as one. Name each force by 'who exerts it on whom'. Weight: Earth on book (gravitational). Push on table: book on table (contact). They are different forces from different interactions and act on different bodies.

items.q: Does any force act on a ball thrown upwards while it is rising, or at the top of its path?
items.correct: Yes. Its weight acts downwards throughout the flight, while rising, at the top and while falling.
items.misconception: Gravity acts on a thrown ball only once it starts to fall, so no force acts while it rises or at the top.
items.why: Students associate gravity with falling, and at the top the ball is momentarily at rest, which seems to mean nothing is acting on it. The Earth's gravitational force depends on the mass of the ball and its position, not on its motion. It acts at every point of the flight, which is why the velocity changes by the same amount each second, upwards or downwards.

items.q: In a collision, does the body whose velocity changes more receive the larger force?
items.correct: No. Both bodies receive forces of equal magnitude. The less massive body has the larger acceleration and larger change in velocity because a = F/m.
items.misconception: The body that is affected more in an interaction (larger change in velocity, more damage) must have received the larger force.
items.why: Students judge force by its visible effect, so a larger effect is taken to mean a larger cause. Separate the force from its effect. The forces are equal (third law); the effect on each body depends on its mass (second law), so the lighter body's velocity changes more.

items.q: Does a rigid floor or table exert a force on a body resting on it?
items.correct: Yes. The surface is slightly compressed and pushes up on the body with the normal force F_N. It is a genuine force, which adjusts in size to what is needed.
items.misconception: A rigid surface such as a floor or table just blocks the body; it is a passive obstacle and cannot exert a force.
items.why: Students associate exerting a force with living things or active agents such as springs, and cannot see a floor deform, so they treat it as merely in the way. This 'obstacles do not exert forces' idea is well documented. Every solid surface deforms slightly under load, like a very stiff spring, and pushes back. That push is the normal force, and it must appear on the free-body diagram of any body in contact with a surface.

items.q: Do two perpendicular forces of 20 N and 15 N have a resultant of 35 N?
items.correct: No. Perpendicular forces combine by Pythagoras: √(20² + 15²) = 25 N.
items.misconception: Perpendicular forces (or components) combine by simple addition.
items.why: Students correctly combine forces along a line by adding them and then apply the same rule to perpendicular forces. Perpendicular vectors form the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle whose hypotenuse is the resultant, so the magnitude is √(F_x² + F_y²), always less than F_x + F_y.

items.q: When two forces act along the same line in opposite directions, are their magnitudes added?
items.correct: No. Forces in opposite directions along a line have opposite signs, so the resultant along that line is their difference.
items.misconception: When some forces are resolved or treated as vectors, forces along the same line are still added without signs, whichever way they point.
items.why: Students add all the numbers that lie along one line without assigning signs for direction, especially when the forces are listed rather than drawn. Choose a positive direction for each line of action and give each force a sign. Opposite forces subtract.

items.q: When a force accelerates two blocks in contact, does each block receive half of the force?
items.correct: No. The resultant force on each block is proportional to its mass, since both have the same acceleration.
items.misconception: When a force accelerates several bodies together, it is shared equally between them.
items.why: Splitting equally is the default when something is 'shared', and students do not connect the force on each block to its mass. Both blocks have the same acceleration, so the resultant force on each is its mass times that acceleration. The heavier block needs the larger share.

items.q: Is the force that block A exerts on block B equal to the resultant force on A?
items.correct: No. The resultant force on A is m_A a; the force A exerts on B is the force needed to accelerate B, m_B a. They are equal only if the masses are equal.
items.misconception: The force a body passes on to another body equals the resultant force on the first body.
items.why: Students calculate one resultant force and then attach it to the wrong body because they do not isolate each block in its own free-body diagram. Draw separate free-body diagrams. For B, the push from A is the only horizontal force, so it equals m_B a. For A, the applied force minus B's push back equals m_A a.

items.q: On an inclined plane, is the weight a component of the normal force, so that F_N cos θ = mg?
items.correct: No. On an incline it is the weight that is resolved: its component perpendicular to the plane is mg cos θ, and F_N balances that component, so F_N = mg cos θ.
items.misconception: On an incline the normal force should be resolved so that its vertical component balances the weight, giving F_N = mg/cos θ.
items.why: Students are used to resolving the angled force and balancing it against a vertical weight, and resolve the wrong force when the surface is tilted. The equation F_N cos θ = mg is correct only when there is no acceleration vertically and no friction, a different situation. Resolve along and perpendicular to the plane. There is no acceleration perpendicular to the plane, so F_N = mg cos θ; the body accelerates (or friction acts) along the plane.

items.q: Is friction on a stationary body calculated with the coefficient of dynamic friction, μ_d?
items.correct: No. μ_d applies only while the surfaces slide over each other. A stationary body experiences static friction, limited by μ_s F_N.
items.misconception: There is a single friction formula, F_f = μF_N, and either coefficient can be used whether or not the body moves.

First decide whether the surfaces are sliding. If they are, F_f = μ_d F_N. If not, F_f is whatever balances the other forces, up to μ_s F_N.

items.q: In Hooke's law, F_H = −kx, is x the length of the spring?
items.correct: No. x is the extension (or compression): the change in length from the natural length.
items.misconception: The x in Hooke's law is the length of the spring.
items.why: The spring's length is the quantity measured directly with a ruler, and students do not subtract the natural length. Extension = stretched length − natural length. An unstretched spring has x = 0 and exerts no elastic force, although its length is not zero.

items.q: Can lengths in cm or mm, or times in ms, be substituted directly into equations whose other quantities are in SI units?
items.correct: No. Every quantity must be in SI base units (m, s, kg) before substitution, or the answer will be wrong by a power of ten.
items.misconception: Values can be substituted in the units given in the question, whatever other units are used in the equation.
items.why: Questions often give convenient units (cm, mm, ms, g) and students copy the numbers straight into the equation without checking units. Convert first: 1 cm = 10⁻² m, 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, 1 ms = 10⁻³ s, 1 g = 10⁻³ kg. Then check that the answer has a sensible size.

items.q: Does the buoyancy force on a fully immersed body increase as it goes deeper?
items.correct: No. For a liquid of constant density, F_b = ρVg is the same at any depth once the body is fully immersed.
items.misconception: Buoyancy increases with depth, because the pressure of the liquid increases with depth.
items.why: Students know that pressure increases with depth and assume the upward force does too. The buoyancy comes from the DIFFERENCE between the pressures on the top and bottom of the body, which does not change with depth. Pressure increases with depth on both the top and bottom surfaces equally, so their difference, and hence the buoyancy, is unchanged. Only the displaced volume, the fluid density and g matter.

items.q: Do astronauts in orbit around the Earth have no weight?
items.correct: No. At the height of the International Space Station the gravitational field strength is still about 90% of its value at the Earth's surface, so astronauts have a large weight; they appear weightless because they are in free fall with their spacecraft.
items.misconception: Astronauts who appear weightless in orbit have no weight, because gravity does not act on them there.
items.why: Astronauts are seen floating in orbit and are described as 'weightless', so students conclude that gravity does not act on them. Every body with mass exerts a gravitational force. In orbit the gravitational force provides the centripetal force that keeps the astronaut and spacecraft falling around the Earth together.

items.q: Does a body's mass decrease when it is taken to the Moon?
items.correct: No. Mass is the amount of matter and the measure of inertia; it does not depend on location. Only weight changes.
items.misconception: A body's mass changes with location, becoming smaller where gravity is weaker.
items.why: Bathroom scales display kilograms but actually respond to weight, so a smaller reading on the Moon looks like a smaller mass. Mass is unchanged anywhere: 70 kg on Earth is 70 kg on the Moon. The weight changes in proportion to g.

items.q: Does gravity need air (an atmosphere) to act?
items.correct: No. Gravity is a field force that acts through empty space; the Sun's gravity holds the Earth in orbit through the vacuum of space.
items.misconception: Gravity acts only where there is air; in a vacuum or in space there is no gravity.
items.why: Students associate the absence of gravity with space, and space with the absence of air, so the two are linked causally. The Moon has no atmosphere, so students who hold this idea expect no gravity there either. Field forces act without contact and without any medium. A feather and a hammer fall with the same acceleration in a vacuum because gravity still acts there and air resistance does not.

items.q: Is the total momentum of a system conserved only if the bodies in it exert no forces on each other?
items.correct: No. Internal forces come in equal and opposite third-law pairs, so they cancel in the total. Momentum is conserved when no resultant EXTERNAL force acts.
items.misconception: Momentum is conserved only when no forces of any kind act, including forces between the bodies in the system.
items.why: Students hear 'no forces act' and do not distinguish internal forces (between parts of the system) from external forces (from outside the system). Collisions and explosions involve large internal forces, yet total momentum is conserved because each internal force has an equal and opposite partner inside the system.

items.q: Is impulse the force divided by the time for which it acts?
items.correct: No. Impulse is force MULTIPLIED by time: J = FΔt, in N s. Dividing momentum change by time gives force, F = Δp/Δt.
items.misconception: Impulse is found by dividing the force by the contact time.
items.why: Students meet F = Δp/Δt and J = FΔt together and mix up which quantity is divided by time. Use the units: N × s = N s, the unit of impulse (and kg m s⁻¹, the unit of momentum). N ÷ s is not a unit of either.

items.q: When a ball bounces back from a wall, is the change in momentum just the momentum it arrived with?
items.correct: No. The wall must first stop the ball and then send it back, so Δp = m(v − u) includes both parts and is larger than mu.
items.misconception: When a body rebounds, its change in momentum equals the momentum needed to stop it; the rebound adds nothing.
items.why: Students picture the impact as 'stopping the ball' and ignore the second half of the contact, when the ball is pushed back out. Use Δp = m(v − u) with signs. Stopping removes mu; rebounding adds mv in the opposite direction, so the magnitude of Δp is m(u + v) for speeds u and v.
items.specStatementText: that the applied external impulse equals the change in momentum of the system

items.q: If a soft surface absorbs a falling body's kinetic energy, does it exert no force on the body?
items.correct: No. To stop the body, the surface must exert a force on it; that force does negative work, transferring the kinetic energy. Force and energy are different quantities.
items.misconception: A soft surface that absorbs a body's kinetic energy only receives the impact; it gives way rather than pushing back, so it exerts no force on the body.
items.why: Cushions visibly give way and "soak up" impacts, so students see them as passive receivers of energy, not as bodies exerting a force; everyday phrases such as "absorbing the impact" reinforce this. Any surface that stops a body must push on it. A soft surface absorbs kinetic energy because its force does negative work on the body; by giving way it makes the force act for longer, and so makes the force smaller, never zero.

items.q: Does all the work done by a conveyor belt on the sand landing on it become kinetic energy of the sand?
items.correct: No. While the sand slides relative to the belt before reaching the belt's speed, friction transfers energy to internal energy. The force is found from momentum, F = v(Δm/Δt); the kinetic-energy gain is only half the work done.
items.misconception: The work done by the belt on the sand all becomes kinetic energy of the sand, so the force can be found from Fv = ½(Δm/Δt)v².
items.why: Students apply energy conservation to find forces and forget that some energy is dissipated while the sand slips before moving with the belt. Use momentum, not energy, to find the force on a changing mass: F = Δp/Δt = v(Δm/Δt). The power delivered is Fv = (Δm/Δt)v², twice the rate at which the sand gains kinetic energy.

items.q: Is the horizontal force needed to move a load equal to the load's weight?
items.correct: No. The weight acts vertically and is supported by the vertical normal force. The horizontal force depends on the horizontal change in momentum (and on friction), not on the weight.
items.misconception: The force needed to move a load is its weight.
items.why: Lifting a load takes a force equal to its weight, and students carry this into horizontal situations where the weight has no component along the motion. In flow problems, students who hold this idea also treat the mass arriving each second as "the load", and multiply the mass flow rate by g. Treat horizontal and vertical directions separately. Horizontally, the belt only has to change the horizontal momentum of the sand: F = v(Δm/Δt).

items.q: Does 'elastic collision' mean a collision involving stretchy materials?
items.correct: No. In physics 'elastic collision' means that total kinetic energy is conserved; the materials need not be stretchy, and a rubber ball can collide inelastically.
items.misconception: An elastic collision is one involving elastic (stretchy) materials such as rubber, and rigid bodies cannot collide elastically.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'elastic' is 'stretchy', as in an elastic band. Use the physics definition: compare total kinetic energy before and after. Hard steel balls can collide almost elastically.

items.q: In an elastic collision, does each body keep its own kinetic energy?
items.correct: No. Kinetic energy is usually transferred between the bodies; it is the TOTAL kinetic energy that is unchanged in an elastic collision.
items.misconception: In an elastic collision each body keeps its own kinetic energy, so if either body's kinetic energy changes the collision is inelastic.
items.why: Students apply the conservation idea to individual bodies rather than to the system, the same error as thinking each body's momentum is conserved. Add the kinetic energies of all the bodies before, and after, and compare the totals. In a collision the whole point is that energy and momentum pass from one body to the other.

items.q: In a totally inelastic collision, where the bodies stick together, is all the kinetic energy lost?
items.correct: No, not unless the total momentum is zero. The combined body still moves with the total momentum, so it keeps kinetic energy ½(m₁ + m₂)v².
items.misconception: When bodies stick together, all their kinetic energy is lost.
items.why: 'Perfectly inelastic' sounds like 'no kinetic energy left', and a car crash in which vehicles stop dead is a memorable image. Find the common velocity from momentum conservation, then the kinetic energy after. Only when the initial total momentum is zero does the combined body stop.

items.q: Is a body's change in kinetic energy equal to ½m(Δv)²?
items.correct: No. ΔE_k = ½mv² − ½mu², which is not the same as ½m(v − u)². Kinetic energies must be calculated separately and then subtracted.
items.misconception: The change in kinetic energy can be found by substituting the change in speed into ½mv².
items.why: Students use the pattern 'change in X' for every quantity and substitute Δv into the kinetic-energy formula. Because E_k depends on v², calculate E_k before and after and subtract. For 6.0 m s⁻¹ to 2.0 m s⁻¹ the factor is 36 − 4 = 32, not (6 − 2)² = 16.

items.q: Can the kinetic energies of fragments moving in opposite directions cancel to zero?
items.correct: No. Kinetic energy is a scalar and ½mv² is never negative, so kinetic energies always add. Only momenta (vectors) can cancel.
items.misconception: Kinetic energy has direction, like momentum, so the kinetic energies of bodies moving in opposite directions cancel.
items.why: Momentum and kinetic energy are both calculated from m and v in the same problems, and students transfer the vector treatment of momentum to energy. E_k = ½mv² contains v², which is positive whichever direction the body moves. Total kinetic energy is the arithmetic sum of all the positive values.

items.q: Does an explosion create energy?
items.correct: No. Energy is transferred from a store in the system (chemical energy of the explosive, or elastic energy of a spring) to kinetic energy, internal energy, light and sound. The total energy of the system is unchanged.
items.misconception: An explosion creates energy, so the total energy of the system increases.
items.why: Everyday language speaks of explosions 'releasing' or 'producing' energy, and the sudden appearance of motion, light and sound looks like new energy. Kinetic energy increases in an explosion because another store decreases. Total energy is conserved.

items.q: Is the centripetal acceleration of a body in uniform circular motion equal to 2πr/T?
items.correct: No. 2πr/T is the speed v, in m s⁻¹. The centripetal acceleration is v²/r = 4π²r/T², in m s⁻².
items.misconception: The quantity 2πr/T (the distance round the circle per unit time) is the acceleration.
items.why: Students confuse the several equations of circular motion and do not check units to distinguish speed from acceleration. Speed = circumference ÷ period. Acceleration = speed² ÷ radius. Check units: m s⁻¹ for speed, m s⁻² for acceleration.
items.specStatementText: that bodies moving along a circular trajectory at a constant speed experience an acceleration that is directed radially towards the centre of the circle—known as a centripetal acceleration as given by a = v²/r = ω²r = 4π²r/T²

items.q: At the lowest point of a vertical circle, does the weight act towards the centre?
items.correct: No. At the lowest point the centre is above the body, so the weight acts away from the centre and the tension must exceed the weight.
items.misconception: The weight always helps to provide the centripetal force, so at every point T + mg = mv²/r.
items.why: The equation T + mg = mv²/r is correct at the TOP of a vertical circle, where both forces act downwards towards the centre, and students reuse it at the bottom. At each point, take 'towards the centre' as positive and give each force its sign. At the top: T + mg = mv²/r. At the bottom: T − mg = mv²/r.

items.q: Is the speed of a point on a rotating wheel equal to its radius divided by the time period?
items.correct: No. In one period the point travels once around the circumference, 2πr, so v = 2πr/T = ωr.
items.misconception: The speed of a point in circular motion is r/T (or r × revolutions per second), without the factor 2π.
items.why: Students confuse revolutions with radians: one revolution is 2π rad, and r/T treats the radius as the distance travelled in one revolution. Distance per revolution = circumference = 2πr. So v = 2πr/T; equivalently ω = 2π/T in rad s⁻¹ and v = ωr.
items.specStatementText: that the motion along a circular trajectory can be described in terms of the angular velocity ω which is related to the linear speed v by the equation as given by v = 2πr/T = ωr.

items.q: Is the angular velocity ω of a wheel the same as the linear speed of a point on its rim?
items.correct: No. ω (rad s⁻¹) is the same for every point on a rigid rotating wheel; the linear speed v = ωr (m s⁻¹) depends on the distance from the axis.
items.misconception: Angular velocity and linear speed are the same quantity, so ω = 2π/T gives the speed of the rim directly.
items.why: Both are called 'velocity' and both are calculated from the period, so students stop after finding ω and attach the units m s⁻¹. Find ω = 2π/T first, then multiply by the radius: v = ωr. Check units: rad s⁻¹ × m = m s⁻¹.

items.q: At a fixed speed, does a larger circle mean a larger centripetal acceleration?
items.correct: No. At a fixed speed a = v²/r, so a larger radius gives a smaller acceleration: a gentle bend needs less acceleration than a tight one. It is at fixed angular velocity that a = ω²r grows with r.
items.misconception: At a given speed, a larger radius means a larger centripetal acceleration, as if a = v²r.
items.why: The form a = ω²r is remembered as 'acceleration grows with radius' and carried over to situations where the speed, not the angular velocity, is fixed; the formula is then mis-recalled as v²r. Choose the form that matches what is held constant: a = v²/r when the speed is fixed, a = ω²r when the angular velocity is fixed. A unit check exposes v²r: (m s⁻¹)² × m = m³ s⁻², not m s⁻².

items.q: Can an angular velocity worked out in degrees per second be used in v = ωr and a = ω²r?
items.correct: No. These equations require ω in radians per second, because they come from the arc-length relation s = rθ, which holds only for θ in radians; one revolution is 360° = 2π rad.
items.misconception: Angular velocity can be worked out in degrees per second and used directly in v = ωr and a = ω²r.
items.why: Degrees are the familiar unit of angle from mathematics classes, and the reason v = ωr needs radians (arc length s = rθ) is rarely revisited once the formula has been learned. Always convert to radians: multiply revolutions by 2π, or degrees by π/180. The radian is dimensionless, which is why ω r in rad s⁻¹ × m gives a speed in m s⁻¹.

items.q: A rope pulls a sledge at 30° above the horizontal. Does the whole tension act to pull the sledge along the ground?
items.correct: No. Only the horizontal component, T cos 30°, acts along the ground; the vertical component, T sin 30°, helps to support the sledge and reduces the normal force.
items.misconception: An angled force contributes its whole magnitude along the direction of motion; the angle can be ignored when finding the resultant.
items.why: Forces are first met acting along the line of motion, and resolving is learned as a separate mathematical procedure that is skipped when the question does not say 'resolve'. Any force not along the chosen axis must be resolved: its component along the axis is F cos θ, where θ is the angle between the force and that axis. Only components along the same line can be added.
